baer-heitev/1:א: (א) From the mother. Since in any case he is a firstborn either for inheritance or for opening the womb for redemption — and for this reason Magen Avraham wrote that one born after miscarriages must fast, for he is a firstborn for inheritance. Accordingly, this requires further study regarding one born by caesarean section and the one born after him, who is not a firstborn either for inheritance or for redemption, whether he must fast — see Kaf HaChayyim. And he wrote in responsum of Maharil siman 14 that firstborn kohanim and leviim must fast on erev Pesach even if he is only a firstborn from the mother, so that he is found not to be a firstborn for inheritance or for redemption — nevertheless he must fast. And see in responsum Shevut Yaakov part 2 siman 16 that one born after a miscarriage of a nine-month son who died within thirty days need not fast — see there. The eldest of the household need not fast even though the plague was also upon them — we are not so stringent, Tur and Maharil. He wrote in Knesset HaGedolah: if there are ten firstborns fasting together, when the shaliach tzibur repeats the prayer he says Aneinu in Shema Koleinu — and Peri Chadash similarly that he should say Aneinu in Shema Koleinu; and Magen Avraham wrote it is not proper to do so, for it is like a public fast.
baer-heitev/1:ב: (ב) Female. Bach wrote it is proper to do so; but in these countries the custom spread per Rama not to fast a firstborn daughter.
baer-heitev/2:א: (א) On Thursday. If erev Pesach falls on erev Shabbat, they fast on erev Shabbat. Maharil wrote in responsum siman 173 that the fast of firstborns must be completed, for it is a public fast — see above siman 249. And if the fast on Thursday is difficult because one may not eat before checking for chametz and some firstborns must check many rooms (and in Shulchan Gavoah it is a mitzvah so he checks well), he tastes a little or commands another to check — Maharil. Maharash HaLevi wrote in Chayei Adam siman 3 that firstborns may eat at a brit milah meal and one who is stringent will come to harm — end of his words. Magen Avraham wrote: and in our country they were stringent. In responsum Chut HaShani siman 25 he wrote that baalei brit, sandak, and father of the boy are permitted to eat at the milah and repay the fast afterward like the Ten Days of Repentance or those fasting on erev Rosh Hashanah, or release a vow. Peri Chadash wrote that one who is lenient with firstborns even without release at a seudat mitzvah did not lose — see there. R' Akiva Eiger wrote: when fasting on behalf of his son, permitted to eat at the milah even one who is not baal brit — see there.
baer-heitev/2:ב: (ב) The mother. Terumat HaDeshen and Maharil wrote she need not fast; where there is distress one may be lenient, especially pregnant or nursing — Magen Avraham and Kaf HaChayyim. However, if she fasted once it is like a vow (as stated in Shekalim, small tractate: if his father began weighing on his behalf, he does not stop). See Kaf HaChayyim. It appears to me simply that if his father fasts for a firstborn from another wife who died and he has another firstborn son to his mother from his second wife, the mother need not fast and his fast counts for both. And similarly if his father has distress and his mother fasts for herself — for those who practice fasting — if she is female, her fast also counts for her son. Kaf HaChayyim.
beer-hagolah/1:א: (א) Tur in the name of Tractate Soferim, last chapter.
beer-hagolah/1:ב: (ב) In the same place, in the name of my father the Rosh and Hagahot Maimoniyot chapter 6.
beer-hagolah/1:ג: (ג) Responsa of Ashkenazim in the name of Sefer HaAgudah.
beer-hagolah/2:א: (א) Terumat HaDeshen, and so too Rokeach and Agur in the name of Mahariv of Molin.
beer-hagolah/2:ב: (ב) In the same place, in the name of his father.
machatzit-hashekel/1:א: (א) Magen Avraham wrote: it appears to me that one born after miscarriages must fast, for he is a firstborn for inheritance — as stated in Choshen Mishpat siman 276 section 6, and these are his words: one born after miscarriages — even though the head of the miscarriage emerged while alive, etc. And similarly a nine-month son whose head emerged and died — the one born after him is firstborn for inheritance. Semag and Shach wrote: that which he wrote "even though the head of the miscarriage emerged while alive" — not specifically the head emerged; rather, the whole emerged alive; nevertheless the one born after him is firstborn for inheritance, unlike responsum She'arit Yosef who holds only the head emerged — see there. Beit Shmuel in Even HaEzer siman 156 note 3: Rambam's view is a live nine-month son (but he wrote it is impossible to know he is nine months unless the husband explained and went far away, and if we fear he came by name — see there) — even if he remained thirty days and died within thirty and also hair and nails were not completed, likewise a complete offspring even rabbinically, and the one born after him is not a firstborn; but doubtful eight-month or nine-month, or even certainly eight-month if he remained thirty days, is offspring even rabbinically, for we say this seven-month is it and he remained in his mother's womb a month more — even if hair and nails were not completed, since he remained thirty days; but if he did not remain thirty days but hair and nails were completed, from the Torah he is also offspring, only rabbinically he is not offspring — see there; also Tosafot's view at least here regarding the fast. One born after an eight-month son whose hair and nails were completed even if he did not remain — need not fast.
machatzit-hashekel/1:ב: (ב) He wrote in Knesset HaGedolah, etc., Aneinu in Shema Koleinu — and see above siman 119 in Magen Avraham note 7 that in Knesset HaGedolah he concludes with "Who answers in time of trouble" and "Who hears prayer." And it is not a conclusion in two; if he concluded only in Shema Koleinu, he has fulfilled.
machatzit-hashekel/1:ג: (ג) For it is a public fast — and he meant: for we hold above siman 429 that even for Rabbeinu Tam there one does not decree a public fast in Nisan; but in Kaf HaChayyim he agreed with Knesset HaGedolah to say Aneinu in Shema Koleinu. In Sefer Ateret Roshe wrote: to resolve this from that siman 429 — in Sheyarei Knesset HaGedolah he reconciles that in siman 429 he said one does not decree a public fast from the month, because they are not obligated; unlike the fast of firstborns, who are obligated and standing. He further wrote in the name of Maharil that also a firstborn who is kohen or levi must fast.
machatzit-hashekel/1:ד: (ד) See there siman 280 page 7 in Magen Avraham siman 280 note 4.
machatzit-hashekel/1:ה: (ה) To eat at a milah meal, etc. — they were stringent; and Kaf HaChayyim wrote in the name of responsum Chut HaShani that baalei brit — meaning father of the son, sandak, and mohel — are permitted to eat and they fast in exchange another day, or release his vow that he regrets having accepted as a vow, and then he need not fast another day.
machatzit-hashekel/1:ו: (ו) And in the name of Ateret Roshe wrote: if he is not a firstborn but fasts on behalf of his son, even if not baal brit — permitted; and Peri Chadash concludes that even one lenient to permit a firstborn who is not baal brit at a milah meal without release did not lose, as Shach wrote in Yoreh Deah siman 234 that one who fasts fasts with awareness it is custom; and behold the custom is to eat on erev Shabbat. But Kaf HaChayyim wrote: and in these countries where the custom is to eat the milah meal at night, one may not be lenient here, as Magen Avraham wrote below siman 559 end of note 11 and in siman 568 note 10; and in my humble opinion perhaps the case is not similar, for on erev Pesach they always make the meal by day, for it is difficult to make it at night.
machatzit-hashekel/2:א: (א) (Note 2) The mother, etc., need not, etc. — for the father's fast on his own behalf also counts for the son. And see siman 550 that also in the three fasts they were lenient regarding pregnant and nursing women.
machatzit-hashekel/2:ב: (ב) That he began, etc. — for even though he is not obligated in half-shekel until he is twenty years old; but if his father began and weighed on behalf of his minor son once, he does not stop again. And he is obligated to weigh from now on.
magen-avraham/1:_: It appears to me that one born after miscarriages must fast, for he is a firstborn for inheritance. Knesset HaGedolah wrote: if there are ten firstborns fasting, the shaliach tzibur says Aneinu in Shema Koleinu; and it appears to me it is not proper to do so, for it is like a public fast — Olat Shabbat siman 280. Maharash HaLevi wrote that firstborns may eat at a brit milah meal, and one who is stringent will come to harm — end of his words; and in our country they were stringent. Thursday: on erev Shabbat one does not fast, as in siman 317; if the fast is difficult for them, they may taste before checking or command another to check (Terumat HaDeshen, Maharil) — see siman 431.
magen-avraham/2:_: The mother fasts. Terumat HaDeshen wrote she need not fast, and so too in Maharil in the name of Maharash; where there is distress one may be lenient, especially pregnant or nursing — siman 559. However, if she fasted once, it is like a vow, as stated in chapter 1 of Shekalim, small tractate: if his father began weighing on his behalf, he does not stop — so in Hagahot Semak siman 144.
magen-avraham/3:_: Istensis — meaning that if he eats by day he will not be hungry at night.
mechaber/1:main: That firstborns fast on erev Pesach. Containing 3 sections: Firstborns fast on erev Pesach, whether a firstborn of the father or of the mother. And some say that even a firstborn daughter fasts. {Rama: (and the custom is not so) (Maharil}.}
mechaber/2:main: If erev Pesach falls on Shabbat, some say the firstborns fast on Thursday; and some say they do not fast at all. {Rama: But one should practice per the first reason, and the custom is: when the father is a firstborn, the mother fasts in place of her firstborn son while he is still a minor; and if the father is not a firstborn, he fasts on behalf of his son until he grows up.}
mechaber/3:main: One who is an istenis fasts on erev Pesach so that he will eat matzah with appetite.
mishnah-berurah/1:א: (א) Firstborns fast — as a remembrance of the miracle that they were saved from the plague of the firstborn.
mishnah-berurah/1:ב: (ב) Whether firstborn of father or mother — the plague of firstborns was on all of them, as stated in the Midrash; nevertheless, the eldest of the household was not required to fast, even though the plague was also upon them. One born after a miscarriage must fast, for he is a firstborn for inheritance; and this is specifically when the miscarriage was certain. But one born after a son of nine months who died within thirty days need not fast. Firstborn kohanim and leviim must also fast, even if they were only firstborns from the mother and are not firstborns for inheritance or redemption — nevertheless they are called firstborn. Maharil wrote that the fast of firstborns must be completed (until tzeit hakochavim, as in siman 249), for it is a public fast. It appears that if one has headache or eye pain, one need not fast. It also appears that if one for whom fasting is difficult cannot eat afterward except light things in very small quantity, it is better not to fast so he can fulfill matzah, maror, and drinking the four cups properly; nevertheless, in both cases it is better he eat only light foods. Firstborns say Aneinu in Shema Koleinu at Minchah when fasting; if ten firstborns pray together and one is shaliach tzibur when repeating the prayer, he says Aneinu in Shema Koleinu as the law of an individual fast — nevertheless l'chatchila the firstborn should not be shaliach tzibur when ten pray together, for some say it is not proper to mention the fast publicly in repetition of the prayer, since it is the month of Nisan.
mishnah-berurah/1:ג: (ג) Even a firstborn daughter — the plague of firstborns was also upon them, as stated in the Midrash.
mishnah-berurah/1:ד: (ד) And the custom is not so — for the Torah did not give sanctity of firstborn status to a female for any matter.
mishnah-berurah/2:א: (א) Erev Pesach on Shabbat — if it falls on erev Shabbat, they fast on that day.
mishnah-berurah/2:ב: (ב) On Thursday — and not on Friday, since it is not a better time to postpone to Friday. If the fast on Thursday is difficult because one must check for chametz at night and sometimes has many rooms to check and may not eat before checking, he tastes a little before checking or commands another to check and they eat.
mishnah-berurah/2:ג: (ג) That they do not fast at all — for this fast is only a custom, since when postponed it is postponed.
mishnah-berurah/2:ד: (ד) When the father is a firstborn — his fast counts for himself.
mishnah-berurah/2:ה: (ה) The mother fasts — and some decisors wrote she need not fast, for the father's fast also counts for the son. Where she suffers distress, one may be lenient, especially if pregnant or nursing; if she suffers from the fast, one may be lenient even if she has no husband to fast for her son. A woman who gives birth every thirty days need not fast for him in any case [per later authorities]. However, if she began once to fast for him, it is like a vow and requires release.
mishnah-berurah/2:ו: (ו) Until he grows up — while the son has not completed thirty days, she need not fast for him. Whether firstborns may eat at a seudat mitzvah depends on local custom; some are stringent. If one wishes to eat at a pidyon haben or brit milah, he needs release (custom is like a vow), except the mohel, sandak, and father of the boy may eat without release, for it is their Festival; they must still repay the fast after Pesach. Some firstborns are lenient and eat at seudat mitzvah; so is practiced today in many places in our country, including at a siyum masechet even if the firstborns did not learn the tractate, since at the one who completes it is a seudat mitzvah and they join his meal.
mishnah-berurah/3:_: (11) Istensis — meaning a delicate person who if he eats by day is not hungry at night. It appears that if erev Pesach is Shabbat, one should not postpone the Shabbat meal entirely for this; only be careful to eat a little to fulfill the seudat mitzvah alone.
